arXiv:1811.09343v1 [math.AP] 23 Nov 2018

Boundedness and stabilization in a two-species chemotaxis system with signal absorption

Qingshan Zhang Address: Department of Mathematics, Henan Institute of Science and Technology, Xinxiang 453003, PR China Email address: qingshan11@yeah.net and Weirun Tao Address: Institute for Applied Mathematics, School of Mathematics, Southeast University, Nanjing 211189, PR China Email address: taoweiruncn@163.com
Abstract.

This paper is concerned with the Neumann initial-boundary value problem for the two-species chemotaxis system with consumption of chemoattractant

{ut=Δu−χ1∇⋅(u∇w),x∈Ω,t>0,vt=Δv−χ2∇⋅(v∇w),x∈Ω,t>0,wt=Δ​w−(α​u+β​v)​w,x∈Ω,t>0\displaystyle\left\{\begin{array}[]{lll}\vskip 6.0pt plus 2.0pt minus 2.0ptu_{t}=\Delta u-\chi_{1}\nabla\cdot(u\nabla w),&{}x\in\Omega,\ t>0,\\ \vskip 6.0pt plus 2.0pt minus 2.0ptv_{t}=\Delta v-\chi_{2}\nabla\cdot(v\nabla w),&{}x\in\Omega,\ t>0,\\ \vskip 6.0pt plus 2.0pt minus 2.0ptw_{t}=\Delta w-(\alpha u+\beta v)w,&{}x\in\Omega,\ t>0\end{array}\right.

in a smooth bounded domain Ω⊂ℝn\Omega\subset\mathbb{R}^{n} (n≥2n\geq 2), where the parameters χ1\chi_{1}, χ2\chi_{2}, α\alpha and β\beta are positive. It is proved that if

max⁡{χ1,χ2}​‖w⁡(x,0)‖L∞​(Ω)<2n​π\max\{\chi_{1},\chi_{2}\}\|w(x,0)\|_{L^{\infty}(\Omega)}<\sqrt{\frac{2}{n}}\pi

the problem possesses a unique global classical solution that is uniformly bounded. Moreover, we prove that

u(x,t)→1|Ω|∫Ωu(x,0),v(x,t)→1|Ω|∫Ωv(x,0)andw(x,t)→0ast→∞u(x,t)\to\frac{1}{|\Omega|}\int_{\Omega}u(x,0),\quad v(x,t)\to\frac{1}{|\Omega|}\int_{\Omega}v(x,0)\quad\mbox{and}\quad w(x,t)\to 0\quad\mbox{as}\ t\to\infty

uniformly with respect x∈Ωx\in\Omega.

Key words and phrases: 
chemotaxis system, global solution, boundedness, stabilization.
2010 Mathematics Subject Classification
35A09, 35B40, 35K55, 92C17.

1. Introduction

In this paper, we deal with the Neumann initial-boundary value problem for the chemotaxis system

{ut=Δu−χ1∇⋅(u∇w),x∈Ω,t>0,vt=Δv−χ2∇⋅(v∇w),x∈Ω,t>0,wt=Δ​w−(α​u+β​v)​w,x∈Ω,t>0,∂u∂ν=∂v∂ν=∂w∂ν=0,x∈∂Ω,t>0,u(x,0)=u0(x),v(x,0)=v0(x),w(x,0)=w0(x),x∈Ω\displaystyle\left\{\begin{array}[]{lll}\vskip 6.0pt plus 2.0pt minus 2.0ptu_{t}=\Delta u-\chi_{1}\nabla\cdot(u\nabla w),&{}x\in\Omega,\ t>0,\\ \vskip 6.0pt plus 2.0pt minus 2.0ptv_{t}=\Delta v-\chi_{2}\nabla\cdot(v\nabla w),&{}x\in\Omega,\ t>0,\\ \vskip 6.0pt plus 2.0pt minus 2.0ptw_{t}=\Delta w-(\alpha u+\beta v)w,&{}x\in\Omega,\ t>0,\\ \vskip 6.0pt plus 2.0pt minus 2.0pt\frac{\partial u}{\partial\nu}=\frac{\partial v}{\partial\nu}=\frac{\partial w}{\partial\nu}=0,&{}x\in\partial\Omega,t>0,\\ \vskip 6.0pt plus 2.0pt minus 2.0ptu(x,0)=u_{0}(x),\quad v(x,0)=v_{0}(x),\quad w(x,0)=w_{0}(x),&{}x\in\Omega\end{array}\right.

in the bounded domain Ω⊂ℝn\Omega\subset\mathbb{R}^{n} (n≥2)(n\geq 2) with smooth boundary, where χ1\chi_{1}, χ2\chi_{2}, α\alpha and β\beta are positive constants, the unknown functions u=u⁡(x,t)u=u(x,t) and v=v⁡(x,t)v=v(x,t) stand for polulation densities and w=w⁡(x,t)w=w(x,t) denotes the concentration of chemoattractant. The symbol ∂∂ν\frac{\partial}{\partial\nu} represents differentiation with respect to the outward normal ν\nu on ∂Ω\partial\Omega. The initial data u0u_{0}, v0v_{0} and w0w_{0} are given positive functions satisfying

(1.7) u0∈C0(Ω¯),v0∈C0(Ω¯)andw0∈W1,q(Ω)u_{0}\in C^{0}(\bar{\Omega}),\quad v_{0}\in C^{0}(\bar{\Omega})\quad\mbox{and}\quad w_{0}\in W^{1,q}(\Omega)

with some q>nq>n.

The model (1) is used in mathematical biology to describe the movement of two populations in respond to the concentration gradient of one common chemical signal. It is a generalization of the famous Keller-Segel system [8]

{ut=Δu−χ∇⋅(u∇w),wt=Δ​w−u​w,\displaystyle\left\{\begin{array}[]{lll}\vskip 6.0pt plus 2.0pt minus 2.0ptu_{t}=\Delta u-\chi\nabla\cdot(u\nabla w),\\ \vskip 6.0pt plus 2.0pt minus 2.0ptw_{t}=\Delta w-uw,\end{array}\right.

which has been studied from a mathematical viewpoint in the last years. It is proved that if n≤2n\leq 2 or

χ​‖w⁡(x,0)‖L∞​(Ω)<16​(n+1)\chi\|w(x,0)\|_{L^{\infty}(\Omega)}<\frac{1}{6(n+1)}

in higher dimensions n≥3n\geq 3, the problem (1) possesses a unique global classical solution which is bounded and satisfies

(1.11) u⁡(x,t)→1|Ω|​∫Ωu0andw⁡(x,t)→0as​t→∞u(x,t)\to\frac{1}{|\Omega|}\int_{\Omega}u_{0}\quad\mbox{and}\quad w(x,t)\to 0\quad\mbox{as}\ t\to\infty

uniformly with respect to x∈Ωx\in\Omega [14, 15, 26]. Moreover, the problem admits at least one global weak solution which is eventually smooth and enjoys the convergence properties (1.11) in bounded convex domain Ω⊂ℝ3\Omega\subset\mathbb{R}^{3} [15]. Recently, some blow-up properties of (1), including blow-up criteria for the local classical solution, lower global blow-up estimate on ‖u‖L∞​(Ω)\|u\|_{L^{\infty}(\Omega)} and local non-degeneracy property for the blow-up points, have been obtained in [6]. Furthermore, global solutions and the stabilization for the corresponding variants of (1), such as chemotaxis-consumption systems with tensor-valued sensitivities [9, 11, 22, 25] and singular sensitivities [24], system (1) with logistic source [10, 1] or coupled chemotaxis-fluid system [12, 21, 20, 23] have also been investigated. For more results on the model variations of (1), we refer to the recent survey [2] and the references therein.

As to the problem (1) with Lotka-Volterra competitive kinetics

{ut=Δu−χ1∇⋅(u∇w)+μ1u(1−u−a1v),x∈Ω,t>0,vt=Δv−χ2∇⋅(v∇w)+μ2v(1−a2u−v),x∈Ω,t>0,wt=Δ​w−(α​u+β​v)​w,x∈Ω,t>0,∂u∂ν=∂v∂ν=∂w∂ν=0,x∈∂Ω,t>0,u(x,0)=u0(x),v(x,0)=v0(x),w(x,0)=w0(x),x∈Ω,\displaystyle\left\{\begin{array}[]{lll}\vskip 6.0pt plus 2.0pt minus 2.0ptu_{t}=\Delta u-\chi_{1}\nabla\cdot(u\nabla w)+\mu_{1}u(1-u-a_{1}v),&{}x\in\Omega,\ t>0,\\ \vskip 6.0pt plus 2.0pt minus 2.0ptv_{t}=\Delta v-\chi_{2}\nabla\cdot(v\nabla w)+\mu_{2}v(1-a_{2}u-v),&{}x\in\Omega,\ t>0,\\ \vskip 6.0pt plus 2.0pt minus 2.0ptw_{t}=\Delta w-(\alpha u+\beta v)w,&{}x\in\Omega,\ t>0,\\ \vskip 6.0pt plus 2.0pt minus 2.0pt\frac{\partial u}{\partial\nu}=\frac{\partial v}{\partial\nu}=\frac{\partial w}{\partial\nu}=0,&{}x\in\partial\Omega,t>0,\\ \vskip 6.0pt plus 2.0pt minus 2.0ptu(x,0)=u_{0}(x),\quad v(x,0)=v_{0}(x),\quad w(x,0)=w_{0}(x),&{}x\in\Omega,\end{array}\right.

it is shown that solutions exist globally and remain bounded if either n=2n=2 [5] or

χi∥w0∥L∞​(Ω)<πn+1,i=1,2\chi_{i}\|w_{0}\|_{L^{\infty}(\Omega)}<\frac{\pi}{\sqrt{n+1}},\quad i=1,2

in the case n≥3n\geq 3 [16], and if a1a_{1}, a2∈(0,1)a_{2}\in(0,1) these solutions satisfy

(u⁡(⋅,t),v⁡(⋅,t),w⁡(⋅,t))→(1−a11−a1​a2,1−a21−a1​a2,0)in​L∞​(Ω)(u(\cdot,t),v(\cdot,t),w(\cdot,t))\to\left(\frac{1-a_{1}}{1-a_{1}a_{2}},\frac{1-a_{2}}{1-a_{1}a_{2}},0\right)\quad\mbox{in}\ L^{\infty}(\Omega)

and if a1≥1>a2a_{1}\geq 1>a_{2},

(u⁡(⋅,t),v⁡(⋅,t),w⁡(⋅,t))→(0,1,0)in​L∞​(Ω)(u(\cdot,t),v(\cdot,t),w(\cdot,t))\to(0,1,0)\quad\mbox{in}\ L^{\infty}(\Omega)

as t→∞t\to\infty [5, 16]. On the other hand, the global existence and stabilization of (weak) solutions to the two-species chemotaxis-fluid system with Lotka-Volterra competitive kinetics have also been established, see e.g. [5, 3, 4, 7]. However, to the best of our knowledge, the problem (1) seems not be investigated yet in the literature.

In the present paper, we prove global existence, boundedness and stabilization of classical solutions to the problem (1). Our main results are stated as follows.

Theorem 1.1.

Let Ω⊂ℝn\Omega\subset\mathbb{R}^{n} (n≥2)(n\geq 2) be bounded domain with smooth boundary and let the parameters χ1,χ2,α,β>0\chi_{1},\chi_{2},\alpha,\beta>0. If

χi∥w0∥L∞​(Ω)<2nπ,i=1,2,\chi_{i}\|w_{0}\|_{L^{\infty}(\Omega)}<\sqrt{\frac{2}{n}}\pi,\quad i=1,2,

then for any initial data u0u_{0}, v0v_{0} and w0w_{0} satisfying (1.7), the problem (1) possesses a unique global classical solution which is bounded in Ω×(0,∞)\Omega\times(0,\infty).

The second result concerns stabilization of the solution provided by Theorem 1.1.

Theorem 1.2.

Under the assumptions of Theorem 1.1, the global classical solution of (1) satisfies

‖u⁡(⋅,t)−u¯0‖L∞​(Ω)→0,\displaystyle\|u(\cdot,t)-\bar{u}_{0}\|_{L^{\infty}(\Omega)}\to 0,
‖v⁡(⋅,t)−v¯0‖L∞​(Ω)→0,\displaystyle\|v(\cdot,t)-\bar{v}_{0}\|_{L^{\infty}(\Omega)}\to 0,
‖w⁡(⋅,t)‖L∞​(Ω)→0\displaystyle\|w(\cdot,t)\|_{L^{\infty}(\Omega)}\to 0

as t→∞t\to\infty, where u¯0:=1|Ω|​∫Ωu0\bar{u}_{0}:=\frac{1}{|\Omega|}\int_{\Omega}u_{0} and v¯0:=1|Ω|​∫Ωv0\bar{v}_{0}:=\frac{1}{|\Omega|}\int_{\Omega}v_{0}.

The rest of the paper is organized as follows. In Section 2, we list some preliminaries. Section 3 is devoted to the proof of Theorem 1.1. Finally, we prove Theorem 1.2 in Section 4.

2. Preliminaries

As a preparation to the proof, we first state one result concerning local existence of classical solution to the problem (1).

Lemma 2.1.

Let u0u_{0}, v0v_{0} and w0w_{0} satisfy (1.7), and let χ1,χ2,α,β>0\chi_{1},\chi_{2},\alpha,\beta>0. Then there exist Tmax≤∞T_{\max}\leq\infty and a uniquely determined triple (u,v,w)(u,v,w) of nonnegative functions

u∈C0​(Ω¯×[0,Tmax))∩C2,1​(Ω¯×(0,Tmax)),\displaystyle u\in C^{0}(\bar{\Omega}\times[0,T_{\max}))\cap C^{2,1}(\bar{\Omega}\times(0,T_{\max})),
v∈C0​(Ω¯×[0,Tmax))∩C2,1​(Ω¯×(0,Tmax)),\displaystyle v\in C^{0}(\bar{\Omega}\times[0,T_{\max}))\cap C^{2,1}(\bar{\Omega}\times(0,T_{\max})),
w∈C0​(Ω¯×[0,Tmax))∩C2,1​(Ω¯×(0,Tmax))∩Ll​o​c∞​([0,Tmax),W1,q​(Ω)),\displaystyle w\in C^{0}(\bar{\Omega}\times[0,T_{\max}))\cap C^{2,1}(\bar{\Omega}\times(0,T_{\max}))\cap L_{loc}^{\infty}([0,T_{\max});W^{1,q}(\Omega)),

which solves (1) in the classical sense. If Tmax<∞T_{\max}<\infty, then

‖u⁡(t)‖L∞​(Ω)+‖v⁡(t)‖L∞​(Ω)+‖w⁡(t)‖W1,q​(Ω)→∞as​t↗Tmax.\|u(t)\|_{L^{\infty}(\Omega)}+\|v(t)\|_{L^{\infty}(\Omega)}+\|w(t)\|_{W^{1,q}(\Omega)}\to\infty\quad\mbox{as}\ t\nearrow T_{\max}.

Furthermore, the solution (u,v,w)(u,v,w) satisfies

(2.1) ‖u⁡(t)‖L1​(Ω)=‖u0‖L1​(Ω)for all​t∈(0,Tm​a​x)\|u(t)\|_{L^{1}{(\Omega)}}=\|u_{0}\|_{L^{1}{(\Omega)}}\quad\mbox{for all}\ t\in(0,T_{max})

and

(2.2) ‖v⁡(t)‖L1​(Ω)=‖v0‖L1​(Ω)for all​t∈(0,Tm​a​x)\|v(t)\|_{L^{1}{(\Omega)}}=\|v_{0}\|_{L^{1}{(\Omega)}}\quad\mbox{for all}\ t\in(0,T_{max})

as well as

(2.3) 0≤w≤‖w0‖L∞​(Ω)in​Ω¯×[0,Tm​a​x).0\leq w\leq\|w_{0}\|_{L^{\infty}(\Omega)}\quad\mbox{in}\ \bar{\Omega}\times[0,T_{max}).
Proof.

The local existence and regularity of the solution is based on standard contraction mapping arguments and parabolic regularity theory, which can be found in [19, Lemma 1.1](see also [14, Lemma 2.1]). Integrating the first and the second equations in (1), we immediately obtain

dd​t​∫Ωu⁡(x,t)​𝑑x=0anddd​t​∫Ωv⁡(x,t)​𝑑x=0\frac{d}{dt}\int_{\Omega}u(x,t)dx=0\quad\mbox{and}\quad\frac{d}{dt}\int_{\Omega}v(x,t)dx=0

which yield (2.1) and (2.2). The statement (2.3) follows from an application of the maximum principle. ∎

The following lemma is a generalization of [25, Lemma 3.2], which asserts that a bound for ‖u‖Lp​(Ω)\|u\|_{L^{p}(\Omega)} and ‖v‖Lp​(Ω)\|v\|_{L^{p}(\Omega)} with p>n2p>\frac{n}{2} for all t∈(0,Tmax)t\in(0,T_{\max}) can guarantee the global existence and boundedness of classical solutions to (1).

Suppose that the initial data u0u_{0}, v0v_{0} and w0w_{0} satisfy (1.7) and the parameters χ1,χ2,α,β>0\chi_{1},\chi_{2},\alpha,\beta>0. Let p≥1p\geq 1. If the first and second components of solution satisfy

(2.4) supt∈(0,Tmax)(‖u⁡(t)‖Lp​(Ω)+‖v⁡(t)‖Lp​(Ω))<∞,\sup_{t\in(0,T_{\max})}\left(\|u(t)\|_{L^{p}(\Omega)}+\|v(t)\|_{L^{p}(\Omega)}\right)<\infty,
